tip: 'Adelante' literally means 'forward' – and it's the standard 'come in!' when someone's at the door (or 'go ahead' anywhere). No verb needed, just wave them onward.
'Estoy hecho polvo' – literally 'I'm made into dust'. Spanish loves physical wreckage for exhaustion, and 'hecho' agrees with the speaker: a woman says 'hecha polvo'.
The friendliest IN the neighborhood? Spanish says OF it: 'el más amable DEL barrio.' After a superlative, English 'in' always becomes 'de.'
'Un bledo' is a worthless weed (pigweed): 'me importa un bledo' = 'it matters a pigweed to me' – i.e. not at all.
'Sorprende' works like 'gusta' – his non-arrival is the subject acting on 'me'. And emotion verbs force subjunctive: that's why it's 'haya llegado', not 'ha llegado'.
'Hay' means 'there is' or 'there are' – it's the same for singular and plural. 'Hay un gato.' 'Hay tres gatos.'
'Lo siento' is literally 'I feel it' – Spanish apologizes by feeling the hurt, not confessing fault. That's why the 'lo' (it) is essential: the thing felt is the point.
'Nos vemos' = 'we see each other' – 'nos' turns 'ver' into a mutual act. English 'see you' only mentions the other person; the Spanish goodbye includes both people.
'Eso' has no gender on purpose: for ideas, situations, or unnamed things, use neuter 'eso', never 'ese'/'esa'. 'Eso es malo' judges the situation, not an object.
You don't ARE your age in Spanish – you HAVE it: 'tengo veinticinco años' = 'I have 25 years'. Saying 'soy veinticinco' sounds like you ARE the number.
'Encantado' agrees with YOU, the speaker: a woman says 'encantada'. It literally means 'enchanted' – Spanish greetings run flowerier than 'nice to meet you'.
'Por' = to get/fetch: 'Fui por pan.' Going somewhere to pick something up.
No English 'do' machinery: Spanish negates by dropping 'no' straight before the verb – 'no como'. There is no don't/doesn't to build first.
'Disculpa' is the 'tú' apology – with a stranger or elder, switch to 'disculpe'. One vowel decides whether you sound friendly or respectful.
Why 'llegues', not 'llegas'? For a future arrival that hasn't happened yet, 'cuando' takes subjunctive. 'Cuando llegas' would mean whenever you habitually arrive.
Spanish packs 'get up very early' into one verb: 'madrugar'. It comes from 'la madrugada', the pre-dawn hours – a named part of the day in Spanish.
'La reunión es importante' uses 'ser': traits that define what something IS take 'ser', not 'estar'.
'Ser' for inherent color: 'El cielo es azul.' Use 'ser' for colors seen as defining traits.
'Idiomas' looks like idioms but means languages – and the trap cuts both ways: an English idiom is 'un modismo'. 'Habla cuatro idiomas' = four languages.
'Por' in math: 'Dos por tres son seis.' 'Por' for multiplication.
Time is plural in Spanish: 'son las tres', because there are three hours. Only one o'clock goes singular – 'es la una'.
'Blanda' isn't bland – it means soft. A 'cama blanda' is a soft bed. Bland, flavorless food is 'soso' in Spanish.
'Ser' + personality adjective: 'Es amable' = kind by nature. 'Ser' describes character – who someone is, not how they currently feel.
Swap the verb and 'seguro' flips meaning: 'estoy seguro' = I'm sure, but 'es seguro' = it's safe. Same adjective – 'ser' or 'estar' decides which one you said.
'Acordarse de' = to remember (always reflexive + 'de'). 'Me acuerdo de ti' = I remember you. Compare: 'acordar' (no 'se') = to agree.
'Riquísima' glues '-ísima' onto 'rica' to max it out ('c' becomes 'qu' to keep the hard sound). Spanish superlatives are welded on, not stacked with 'very very'.
Descriptive adjectives usually trail their noun: 'restaurante italiano', never 'italiano restaurante'. The noun comes first; the adjective follows to describe it.
Spanish counts the family from the inside: 'somos cinco', literally 'we are five'. No 'there are five of us' – the group itself speaks as 'we'.
Why 'de color naranja'? 'Naranja' is really the fruit name used as a color, so it never agrees – no 'naranjas' for orange things. 'Rosa' and 'violeta' work the same way.
Present tense for scheduled events: 'La reunión empieza a las tres.' Spanish uses present tense for fixed schedules, like 'El tren sale a las 8.'
